![Ten archipelago sub-regions and 91 catalogued habitation sites across Island Melanesia, Fiji and Micronesia from 10000BC to 1850.](figures/precolonial_melanesia_micro_regional_map.png)



# Abstract

Between the terminal Pleistocene in 10000BC and the eve of formal European partition in 1850, human settlement across Island Melanesia and Micronesia expanded from a single Pleistocene foothold in Near Oceania into ten distinct maritime archipelago populations totalling 606,5k (606.500) inhabitants across 220.891,8 km² of buffered insular space (mean density 2,75 inhabitants per km²). At 10000BC, only the Main Solomon Islands chain from Buka to Guadalcanal held a documented population (8k), whereas the entire oceanic expanse east of Makira and north of the equator remained uninhabited [@sheppard2011lapita; @carson2014first]. Two independent maritime leaps broke this Pleistocene threshold: an open-ocean voyage from the northern Philippines established the first settlements in the Mariana Islands around 1500BC (reaching 6k inhabitants), followed between 1100BC and 850BC by the rapid Lapita expansion out of the Bismarck Archipelago across Temotu (4,5k), Vanuatu (18k), New Caledonia (14k) and Fiji (16k), alongside early western Micronesian settlement in Palau and Yap (8k) [@clark2009radiocarbon; @pugach2020ancient; @anonymous2019debating; @liu2022ancient]. By 1AD, emergent coral reef flats allowed colonisation of the Central-Eastern Carolines (16k), the Marshall Islands (6,5k) and the Gilbert Islands with Nauru (12k), lifting the full ten-archipelago aggregate to 338k inhabitants, divided exactly three-to-one between Island Melanesia with Fiji (253,5k, 75%) and Micronesia (84,5k, 25%) [@rainbird2004archaeology; @kirch2010lapita]. Subsequent horticultural intensification, irrigated taro terracing, fortified chiefly confederacies and basalt-megalithic states pushed the regional total to 487,3k by 1000AD and 601,5k by 1650 [@anonymous2009early; @anderson2009faunal]. Between 1650 and 1850, headline growth appeared nearly static at +0,8% only because Spanish conquest, mission concentration and Old World epidemics reduced the Mariana Islands by 77,4% from 42k to 9,5k, masking continued expansion in Fiji and Rotuma (145k), the Main Solomons (135k), Vanuatu (115k), New Caledonia and the Loyalty Islands (65k), the Carolines (80k combined) and the central Pacific atolls (46k). Reconciling archaeological chronologies, ancient genomic turnovers, historical geographic polygon series and a gazetteer of 91 catalogued settlements across 12 modern territories yields a continuous demographic baseline for the pre-colonial western Pacific.

# Background

## Near Oceania and the Pleistocene Boundary

The demographic geography of the western Pacific rests on one of the sharpest biogeographic frontiers on Earth: the boundary separating Near Oceania from Remote Oceania [@kirch2017road; @sheppard2011lapita; @carson2014first]. Near Oceania encompasses New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago and the Main Solomon Islands as far southeast as Makira (San Cristobal). During the Late Pleistocene, lowered glacio-eustatic sea levels fused Bougainville, Choiseul, Santa Isabel and Guadalcanal into a single Greater Bukida landmass separated from New Ireland by intervisible water gaps under 180 km wide. Modern humans crossed those straits by at least 29000BP, leaving deep Pleistocene strata at Kilu Cave on Buka Island alongside evidence of wild *Colocasia* taro processing, reef fishing and rainforest hunting [@wickler1988pleistocene; @sheppard2011lapita; @kirch2010lapita].

East of Makira and north of the equator lay Remote Oceania. Reaching the Reef and Santa Cruz Islands (Temotu) required a 350 km blind open-water voyage out of sight of land, while reaching the Marianas from Island Southeast Asia demanded an unbroken crossing exceeding 2.000 km across the Philippine Sea [@carson2014first; @clark2009radiocarbon; @hung2011first]. Beyond this threshold, terrestrial biodiversity dropped precipitously: native land mammals vanished except for bats, malaria-bearing *Anopheles* mosquitoes disappeared east of Vanuatu and north of New Guinea, and oceanic islands offered pristine rookeries of flightless rails, megapodes, giant tortoises and terrestrial crocodiles awaiting naive predation [@steadman1995prehistoric; @irwin2011further; @anderson2009faunal; @hawkins2026vanuatu]. For the first eight millennia of the Holocene, therefore, Remote Oceania remained completely empty of human inhabitants.

## Pioneer Marianas Settlement and the Five Micronesian Streams

The first human crossing into Remote Oceania occurred not in Melanesia, but in the western North Pacific. Radiocarbon sequences from Unai Bapot on Saipan, Taga on Tinian and Ritidian on Guam place initial settlement of the Mariana Islands around 1500BC, accompanied by thin red-slipped, lime-infilled pottery closely related to Neolithic assemblages of northern Luzon and Wallacea [@hung2011first; @clark2009radiocarbon; @carson2014first; @ono2025early]. Ancient genomes recovered from Guam and Saipan confirm that the earliest Chamorro voyagers derived directly from Austronesian-speaking populations of the northern Philippines, sharing an ultimate ancestral link with the early Lapita dispersal yet following an independent northern route [@pugach2020ancient; @liu2022ancient; @spriggs2011archaeology].

Micronesia as a whole was never peopled by a single homogeneous wave. Genome-wide analyses identify five distinct prehistoric migration streams across the region, characterised by strong matrilocal residence patterns among early seafaring communities [@liu2022ancient; @gray2009language]. Following the 1500BC Marianas crossing, western Micronesian voyagers settled Palau and Yap by roughly 1000BC, introducing upland terrace agriculture, early coastal burials and pottery to Babeldaob and Yap while gradually receiving secondary Papuan-related gene flow from the northern New Guinea rim [@fitzpatrick2003early; @liston2009cultural; @rainbird2004archaeology; @liu2022ancient]. Farther east, low coral atolls of the Marshall and Gilbert chains remained largely submerged beneath the mid-Holocene highstand until sea-level drawdown exposed habitable reef islets during the late first millennium BC. Only then did Nuclear Micronesian-speaking seafarers expanding northward out of the southeast Solomons and northern Vanuatu settle Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, the Marshalls and the Gilberts, establishing all ten regional populations by 1AD [@rainbird2004archaeology; @liu2022ancient; @sear2026how].

## The Lapita Expansion and Post-Lapita Population Turnover

South of the equator, the demographic map was transformed between 1100BC and 850BC by the Lapita Cultural Complex. Emerging in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1350BC at staging hubs such as Tamuarawai on Emirau Island, Lapita combined finely dentate-stamped earthenware, shell-working in *Conus* and *Tridacna*, obsidian exchange networks, domesticated pigs, dogs and chickens, and outrigger canoe voyaging capable of tacking upwind into the southeast trades [@kirch1988longdistance; @specht2014deconstructing; @summerhayes2009tamuarawai; @szabo2010shell; @anonymous2019debating; @os2025ancient]. Remarkably, early Lapita colonists largely bypassed the already inhabited Main Solomon Islands, leapfrogging directly across the Near-Remote Oceania gap into the Reef and Santa Cruz Islands (Nenumbo and Nanggu) before exploding across Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji within barely five to eight generations [@sheppard2011lapita; @kirch2010lapita; @cochrane2021using].

Excavations at Teouma on Efate, Uripiv and Vao off Malakula, Site 13 at Koné (Lapita) in New Caledonia, and Bourewa, Natunuku, Naigani and Yanuca in Fiji document the remarkable speed and ecological impact of this founding horizon [@bedford2006teouma; @bedford2008northern; @sand1997chronology; @clark2001pattern; @bedford2011lapita; @irwin2011further; @anonymous2009early; @anderson2009faunal]. Stable isotope analyses of the Teouma cemetery burials show that first-generation pioneers combined intensive marine reef foraging with rapid predation on naive terrestrial fauna and nascent root-crop horticulture, while practising complex multi-stage mortuary rituals involving skull removal [@bentley2007lapita; @kinaston2014lapita; @valentin2016flexions]. Within two centuries of landing, colonists extinguished endemic tortoises, terrestrial crocodiles (*Mekosuchus*), giant flightless birds (*Sylviornis*) and numerous landbirds across New Caledonia, Vanuatu and Fiji, compelling an irreversible pivot toward intensive arboriculture and yam-taro gardening [@steadman1995prehistoric; @anderson2009faunal; @irwin2011further; @field2026prey; @hawkins2026vanuatu].

From Fiji, eastern Lapita voyagers pushed rapidly to Nukuleka in Tonga and Mulifanua in Samoa by 900BC to 850BC, laying the ancestral foundation of Polynesia [@burley2001origin; @burley2010nukuleka; @petchey2001radiocarbon; @petchey2019importance; @mclean2008were]. Behind them in Vanuatu and Island Melanesia, however, an extraordinary demographic transformation unfolded after 500BC. Ancient DNA from Vanuatu demonstrates that while initial Lapita pioneers carried overwhelmingly East Asian Austronesian ancestry, subsequent sustained migration streams out of the Bismarck Archipelago and the Solomons introduced predominant Papuan-related genetic ancestry into Vanuatu and southern Island Melanesia without displacing local Oceanic Austronesian languages [@skoglund2016genomic; @lipson2018population; @posth2018language]. This continuous genetic and cultural circulation knit Near and Remote Melanesia into a dense horticultural continuum while leaving Polynesia genetically distinct to the east.

## Agricultural Intensification, Chiefdoms and Megalithic Polities

Between 1AD and 1650, regional populations across Island Melanesia and Micronesia rose by nearly 80% as societies engineered productive island landscapes. In New Caledonia, Kanak communities sculpted monumental irrigated wetland taro terraces (*tarodières*) across the mountain valleys of Grande Terre and constructed dry-stone fortifications on Maré, while cultivating raised yam mounds along dry western plains [@sand1997chronology; @anderson2009faunal]. In southern Vanuatu, Aneityum and Tanna supported dense canal-fed taro irrigation systems capable of sustaining thousands of inhabitants on compact volcanic valleys [@bedford2008northern; @hawkins2026vanuatu]. In Fiji, demographic growth after AD 1000 coincided with climatic instability, upland settlement retreat and the proliferation of lowland ring-ditch fortifications (*koro waiwai*) across the Rewa and Sigatoka deltas, culminating by the late eighteenth century in competing maritime confederacies (*matanitu*) centred on Verata, Rewa, Bau, Somosomo and Lakeba [@field2004environmental; @anonymous2009early; @cochrane2010evidence; @king2026local; @field2026prey].

Parallel state-like and chiefdom hierarchies crystallised across Micronesia. In the Mariana Islands, the *latte* period (AD 900 to 1668) saw coastal and upland villages organised around paired limestone and basalt pillar foundations (*haligi* and *tasa*) supporting elite dwellings and canoe houses across Guam, Tinian, Saipan and Rota [@rainbird2004archaeology; @carson2014first]. On Babeldaob in Palau, vast stepped earthwork terraces constructed during the first millennium AD gave way after AD 1200 to nucleated coastal stone-path villages (*bai* complexes) such as Koror and Melekeok amid ongoing scholarly debate over whether the climatic transition around AD 1300 forced that realignment [@liston2009cultural; @fitzpatrick2010critique; @nunn2010defending]. Farther east, basalt-megalithic dynasties rose on the high volcanic islands of Pohnpei and Kosrae: the Saudeleur rulers constructed 92 artificial prismatic-basalt islets at Nan Madol on Pohnpei's eastern reef flat between AD 1200 and 1600, while the Tokosra paramounts erected the walled coral-and-basalt compound of Leluh on Kosrae, governing island-wide tribute networks [@mccoy2016nanmadol; @rainbird2004archaeology]. Even on narrow coral atolls in the Marshall and Gilbert chains, excavated *Cyrtosperma* swamp-taro pits, breadfruit groves and institutionalised council houses (*maneaba*) sustained remarkably high dry-land densities until European whalers, sandalwooders and colonial garrisons arrived [@rainbird2004archaeology; @sear2026how].

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Partitioning and Buffered Insular Geometry

Because Island Melanesia and Micronesia span more than 6.000 km of open ocean across hundreds of volcanic arcs, raised coral limestone islands and low-lying atolls, regional demographic accounting requires partitioning the basin into ten ecologically and culturally coherent archipelago sub-regions: five in Island Melanesia and Fiji (Main Solomon Islands including Bougainville, Temotu-Santa Cruz Islands, Vanuatu Archipelago, New Caledonia and Loyalty Islands, Fiji and Rotuma) and five in Micronesia (Mariana Islands of Guam and the Northern Marianas, Western Carolines of Palau and Yap, Central-Eastern Carolines of Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, Marshall Islands, and Gilbert Islands with Nauru).

A critical geometric distinction governs spatial density calculations across oceanic archipelagos. In the chapter areal mask, small islands and dispersed coral atolls are represented with standardised coastal buffer halos so that every inhabited archipelago retains a contiguous polygon footprint on global historical maps. Total buffered mask area across the ten sub-regions equals 220.891,8 km², divided into 168.933,1 km² across Island Melanesia and Fiji and 51.958,7 km² across Micronesia. True emergent dry-land area is substantially smaller: historical geographic polygon tables record 37.616 km² for the Main Solomons (including Bougainville), 18.810 km² for New Caledonia and the Loyalties, 15.334 km² for Fiji and Rotuma, 12.438 km² for Vanuatu and 669 km² for Temotu, while all five Micronesian archipelagos combined possess barely 2.700 km² of emergent land despite spanning 51.958,7 km² of buffered maritime-insular mask. Throughout this chapter, table densities report standardised mask densities (matching the regional charts) while the analytical text pairs them with true dry-land densities wherever atoll carrying capacity is assessed.

## Archaeological Anchors, Back-Projection and Benchmark Harmonisation

Pre-colonial benchmark populations across 10000BC, 1500BC, 1000BC, 1AD, 1000AD, 1650 and 1850 are constructed by synthesising three evidentiary tiers rather than relying on any single proxy. First, for the founding horizons (10000BC to 1AD), presence and absence are fixed strictly by calibrated radiocarbon chronologies, marine reservoir corrections and palaeofaunal extinction horizons [@clark2009radiocarbon; @sheppard2011lapita; @petchey2019importance; @anderson2009faunal]. In the raw archaeological benchmark specification, nine of the ten sub-regions stand at exactly 0 inhabitants in 10000BC, leaving only the Main Solomons inhabited at 8k. The Mariana Islands enter the occupied ledger at 1500BC (6k), followed at 1000BC by Temotu (4,5k), Vanuatu (18k), New Caledonia (14k), Fiji and Rotuma (16k) and the Western Carolines (8k). The Central-Eastern Carolines (16k), Marshalls (6,5k) and Gilberts with Nauru (12k) enter full settlement visibility by 1AD.

Second, for the first and second millennia AD, regional curves integrate archaeological settlement-density proxies—fortified ring-ditch counts in the Rewa and Sigatoka valleys, Kanak *tarodière* terrace footprints, Chamorro *latte* village surveys, Palauan earthwork-to-coastal-village sequences and basalt monumental labour requirements at Nan Madol and Leluh—with island carrying-capacity bounds [@rainbird2004archaeology; @anonymous2009early; @fitzpatrick2010critique; @cochrane2021using]. Third, for the closing pre-colonial benchmarks (1650 and 1850), totals are anchored backward from earliest systematic missionary enumerations (such as the 1848 Aneityum census of 3.513 inhabitants), Spanish colonial padrón rolls in the Marianas (1710 to 1830), early naval survey estimates (including the 1840–1841 United States Exploring Expedition across Fiji and the Gilberts) and nineteenth-century colonial baselines (Fiji 1881, New Caledonia 1887, Guam and Micronesian administrative enumerations), adjusting explicitly for documented contact-era epidemic losses.

An important technical feature of the summary cache series requires explicit notation. When interpolating sparse prehistoric tables onto a uniform seven-epoch grid, the automated cache clamps each sub-region's earliest non-zero benchmark backward across earlier columns, yielding nominal cache totals of 109k at 10000BC, 143k at 1500BC and 156,2k at 1000BC. Those pre-1AD cache figures represent backwards-clamped mathematical floors, not pre-Lapita human occupation of Remote Oceania. From 1AD through 1850, once all ten archipelagos are settled, the raw archaeological series and the harmonised benchmark cache coincide identically at 338k (1AD), 487,3k (1000AD), 601,5k (1650) and 606,5k (1850).

## Settlement Gazetteer Compilation and Provenance Discipline

To ground sub-regional curves in concrete places, the companion gazetteer compiles 91 habitation centres and 238 time-stamped population observations spanning 10000BC to 1850 across 12 modern national and territorial jurisdictions. Ingestion proceeded in four tracked waves logged in the chapter source ledger: Wave 1 harvested 20 primary colonial and national census baselines (including Spanish Marianas rolls and early Pacific territorial registers); Wave 2 contributed 70 settlements from peer-reviewed archaeological monographs and ethnohistorical surveys (led by excavations at Kilu, Teouma, Mangaasi, Koné, Sigatoka, Bourewa, Natunuku, Naigani, Unai Bapot, Taga, Nan Madol, Leluh and Roviana); Wave 3 performed longitudinal deduplication without adding unattested aliases; and Wave 4 executed a sub-regional gap sweep adding one final node (marginal gain 1,11%). One out-of-bounds candidate (Yela in Louisiade, Papua New Guinea, at -11,35°S, 154,17°E) was excluded outside the chapter mask, leaving zero unaccounted candidates, zero empty sub-regions and a 0% crowd-sourced fallback share.

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciling Raw Archaeological Floors, Harmonised Series and Gridded Rasters

Internal consistency across the chapter is tested along three independent axes: raw archaeological onset versus harmonised regional trajectories, archival HGIS polygon sums versus regional totals, and continuous 5-arcminute spatial raster aggregates versus tabular archipelago headcounts. Two critical validation diagnostics emerge directly from Table \ref{tab:benchmark-validation}. First, across the five larger volcanic and continental-fragment archipelagos of Island Melanesia and Fiji, the 5-arcminute spatial raster matches the regional benchmark sum with remarkable fidelity: 466.821 raster inhabitants against 471.000 tabular inhabitants in 1850 (99,1% closure). Exact 100% alignment holds in the Main Solomons (135.000), Temotu (11.000) and Vanuatu (115.000), while minor coastline-clipping losses appear in New Caledonia (64.932 against 65.000, -0,1%) and Fiji with Rotuma (140.889 against 145.000, -2,8%, reflecting small Lau and Rotuma outlier islands clipped by grid cells).

Second, all five Micronesian sub-regions register exactly 0 in the global 5-arcminute land-raster across every time slice from 10000BC to 1850, accounting for the entire 139.679 gap between the 1850 raster total (466.821) and the full regional total (606.500). Because individual coral atolls and small high islands in the Marianas, Carolines, Marshalls and Gilberts frequently measure less than 1 to 15 km across, their dry-land area drops below the land-fraction threshold of standard 5-arcminute global rasters. Cross-checking against the 112-row HGIS regime table confirms that Micronesian demography must be reconstructed from island-level historical polygon archives (9 Micronesian administrative units summing to 86,5k in 1AD, 120,4k in 1000AD, 142,7k in 1500 and 86,1k in 1840) rather than raw gridded global population models.

## Cross-Checking against Independent Radiocarbon, Isotopic and Genomic Evidence

External cross-checks test whether our regional trajectories respect independent bioarchaeological constraints. Chronologically, the abrupt step from 8k in 10000BC to 48k active in 1500BC and 121,7k active in 1000BC mirrors the sharp radiocarbon onset of Bapot-1 in Saipan [@clark2009radiocarbon], Teouma and Malakula in Vanuatu [@bedford2011lapita; @kinaston2014lapita], Pindai and Koné in New Caledonia [@anderson2009faunal], and Bourewa, Naigani and Sigatoka in Fiji [@irwin2011further; @cochrane2010evidence; @anonymous2009early]. Ecologically, the subsequent doubling from 121,7k in 1000BC to 338k in 1AD tracks the well-dated transition from coastal reef-and-megafauna exploitation to inland root-crop horticulture and pig husbandry documented by isotopic studies on Efate and Waya Island and ancient pig mitogenomes across Remote Oceania [@kinaston2014lapita; @king2026local; @os2025ancient; @field2026prey]. Genetically, steady first-millennium growth in Vanuatu (58k to 84k) and the Main Solomons (78k to 104,9k) aligns with ancient DNA evidence of sustained Near-to-Remote Oceania migration rather than demographic collapse after Lapita [@lipson2018population; @posth2018language]. Finally, the sharp 1650 to 1850 contraction in the Marianas (42k down to 9,5k) matches Spanish colonial enumeration rolls showing Hagåtña falling from 3.000 in 1668 to 1.648 in 1710 before recovering gradually to 3.100 by 1830 through forced concentration of outer-island survivors onto Guam [@rainbird2004archaeology].

# Results

## Long-Run Demographic Trajectory (10000BC to 1850)

Across the twelve millennia examined in this chapter, Island Melanesia and Micronesia evolved from a single Near Oceanic Pleistocene frontier into a densely settled oceanic world of 606,5k inhabitants. Figure \ref{fig:melanesia-trajectory} plots the aggregate trajectory alongside the four largest Melanesian archipelagos (Panel A) and ranks all ten sub-regions by 1850 areal mask density (Panel B).

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:melanesia-trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-precolonial-melanesia-micro/precolonial_melanesia_micro_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:melanesia-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Regional population trajectory for Island Melanesia and Micronesia and its four largest archipelagos from 10000BC to 1850 (Panel A) and sub-regional areal mask density rankings in 1850 (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

Three macro-phases divide this curve. During the long pre-Lapita phase (10000BC to 1500BC), active human population remained tiny and geographically confined: the Main Solomons expanded gradually from 8k Pleistocene rainforest and coastal foragers to 42k horticulturalists by 1500BC as taro, yam and tree-crop cultivation matured across Near Oceania, joined around 1500BC by 6k pioneer Chamorro settlers in the Marianas [@sheppard2011lapita; @clark2009radiocarbon; @carson2014first]. During the oceanic colonisation phase (1100BC to 1AD), maritime expansion across Remote Oceania multiplied active regional headcount sevenfold from 48k to 338k in barely fifteen centuries. By 1AD, every habitable archipelago from Palau to Fiji and from the Marianas to the Gilberts sustained reproducing island populations.

During the agrarian and chiefly intensification phase (1AD to 1650), total population rose steadily at an implied compound rate of roughly 0,035% per year, climbing from 338k in 1AD to 487,3k in 1000AD (+44,2%) and 601,5k in 1650 (+23,4%). Between 1650 and 1850, however, the two halves of the western Pacific diverged sharply. Island Melanesia and Fiji continued growing from 440,2k to 471k (+7%), lifting their share of the chapter total from 73,2% to 77,7%. Micronesia as a whole contracted by 16% from 161,3k to 135,5k—entirely driven by the catastrophic colonial depopulation of the Mariana Islands (-77,4%, a loss of 32,5k inhabitants), even as the Carolines, Marshalls and Gilberts added 6,7k inhabitants prior to sustained colonial annexation. Table \ref{tab:subregional-matrix} summarises all ten sub-regions from 1AD to 1850.

## Island Melanesia: Solomons, Temotu, Vanuatu and New Caledonia

The Main Solomon Islands including Bougainville (64.835,2 km² mask; 37.616 km² dry land) anchored the chapter's earliest demographic continuity and remained its second-largest population centre in 1850. Rising from 8k in 10000BC and 42k in 1500BC to 78k in 1AD (23,1% of the chapter total), the archipelago expanded to 104,9k in 1000AD, 127,2k in 1650 and 135k in 1850 (22,3% share; 2,08 inhabitants per km² of mask, or 3,59 per km² of dry land). Across its 12 catalogued settlements, population clustered along two complementary ecological belts: fertile southern plains of Bougainville exemplified by Buin (2.860 in 1800) alongside the ancient Buka sequence at Kilu (790 by 1500), and defensive coastal lagoons of New Georgia and Malaita where maritime polities such as Roviana (2.350), Marovo (1.580), Bilua (1.540) and the artificial coral-rubble shell-money islets of Langa Langa (1.850) and Sulufou (580) flourished [@sheppard2011lapita; @szabo2010shell]. Interior highlands of Guadalcanal and Malaita remained sparsely settled because endemic malaria and steep karst terrain constrained density below coastal carrying capacity.

Immediately across the Near-Remote Oceania sea gap, the compact Temotu and Santa Cruz Islands (2.866,9 km² mask; 669 km² dry land) acted as the indispensable Lapita stepping-stone [@sheppard2011lapita; @kirch2010lapita]. Uninhabited before Lapita colonists landed at Nenumbo (peaking at 485) and Nanggu (890) around 1050BC, Temotu reached 4,5k by 1000BC, 7,5k by 1AD, 9,2k by 1000AD and 11k by 1850 (1,8% share; 3,84 per km² of mask, but a steep 16,44 inhabitants per km² of dry land). Remarkably, this tiny province also absorbed later Polynesian outlier communities on Tikopia (Matautu reaching 1.190 under strict zero-growth agroforestry management) and Anuta (138), alongside the populous Nendo anchorage of Graciosa Bay (1.420 in 1595 when Mendaña arrived), documented across 7 catalogued locales.

Southward, the volcanic Vanuatu Archipelago (27.610,8 km² mask; 12.438 km² dry land) experienced rapid Lapita foundation at Teouma on Efate, Avunatari on Malo, Ifo on Erromango and Uripiv off Malakula [@kinaston2014lapita; @bedford2011lapita; @hawkins2026vanuatu]. From zero at 1500BC, Vanuatu surged to 18k by 1000BC, 58k by 1AD (17,2% share), 84k by 1000AD, 106,8k by 1650 and 115k by 1850 (19% share; 4,17 inhabitants per km² of mask, third highest in the study, and 9,25 per km² of dry land). After initial Lapita settlers experienced genetic admixture and replacement from Near Oceanic streams [@lipson2018population; @posth2018language], local communities engineered intensive dryland yam and irrigated taro economies across Efate (Mangaasi, seat of the renowned Roi Mata domain at 1.080 in 1600), Tanna (Port Resolution at 2.650 in 1774) and Aneityum, where Anelgauhat and its irrigated valley catchments registered 3.513 inhabitants in the 1848 missionary census before introduced measles and dysentery devastated the southern islands.

New Caledonia and the Loyalty Islands (34.896,9 km² mask; 18.810 km² dry land) combined continental ultramafic geology on Grande Terre with raised coral limestone platforms in Lifou, Maré and Ouvéa. Settled by Lapita pioneers at Koné (Site 13, 650 by 1000AD), Tiouandé (910) and Vao on the Isle of Pines (1.380) around 1050BC, human arrival triggered swift megafaunal extinctions documented at the Pindai Caves [@anderson2009faunal]. Population climbed from 14k in 1000BC to 42k in 1AD (12,4% share), 53,2k in 1000AD, 62k in 1650 and 65k in 1850 (10,7% share; 1,86 per km² of mask, or 3,46 per km² of dry land). Because infertile nickel-bearing serpentine soils blanketed much of central and southern Grande Terre, Kanak demography concentrated heavily along irrigated northeastern mountain valleys such as Hienghène (2.100 in 1800) and Balade (1.240 in 1774) and on the malaria-free Loyalty Islands, where Wé on Lifou (2.340), Tadine on Maré (1.840) and Fayaoué on Ouvéa (1.490) sustained dense yam-and-coconut chiefdoms across 9 catalogued centres.

## Fiji and Rotuma: Ring-Ditch Fortifications and Matanitu Confederacies

By 1850, Fiji and Rotuma (38.723,3 km² mask; 15.334 km² dry land) stood as the demographic colossus of the entire western Pacific study domain. Uninhabited prior to Lapita landfall around 1000BC at Bourewa (590), Natunuku (710), Yanuca (164) and Naigani (188) [@irwin2011further; @anonymous2009early; @cochrane2010evidence], the archipelago climbed steeply from 16k in 1000BC to 68k in 1AD (20,1% share), 102,4k in 1000AD (21%), 133,6k in 1650 and 145k in 1850 (23,9% share; 3,74 inhabitants per km² of mask, and 9,46 per km² of dry land).

Unlike malaria-burdened western Melanesia, Fiji lay outside the *Anopheles* zone, permitting dense nucleated habitation along fertile alluvial deltas and windward river valleys. Archaeological surveys and isotopic studies from Waya Island and the Sigatoka Sand Dunes (rising from 240 in 800BC to 1.120 in 1820) trace a decisive transition after AD 1000 from dispersed coastal hamlets toward defensive hilltop forts and hundreds of lowland ring-ditch fortifications (*koro waiwai*) carved across the wet Rewa delta [@cochrane2010evidence; @king2026local; @field2026prey; @anonymous2009early]. By the late eighteenth century, political consolidation produced major competing confederacies (*matanitu*): Verata peaked at 2.200 in 1700 before yielding primacy to the rival Kubuna capital on tiny reclaimed Bau Island (3.500 in 1840) and the Burebasaga delta metropolis of Rewa (3.600 in 1840), flanked by regional seats at Somosomo on Taveuni (1.620), Tubou on Lakeba in the Lau Group (1.480), Tavuki on Kadavu (1.780) and Macuata on Vanua Levu (1.250), alongside the fertile Polynesian-affiliated volcanic outlier of Rotuma (Motusa at 2.680 in 1820). Together, Fiji and Rotuma contribute 14 catalogued settlements—the second largest national count in our gazetteer after the Solomon Islands.

## Micronesia: Latte Villages, Megalithic Chiefdoms and Atoll Ceilings

Across the five Micronesian sub-regions, compact volcanic high islands and razor-thin coral atolls produced striking contrasts in both pre-colonial density and historical vulnerability. Figure \ref{fig:melanesia-hierarchy} illustrates how prominently Micronesian centres rank among the largest recorded settlements in the western Pacific, with Gagil-Tomil on Yap (4.120), Utiroa on Tabiteuea (3.850), Kitti on Pohnpei (3.120) and Hagåtña on Guam (3.100) standing directly alongside Rewa, Anelgauhat and Bau at the apex of the 91-site hierarchy.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:melanesia-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-precolonial-melanesia-micro/precolonial_melanesia_micro_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:melanesia-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Twelve largest catalogued settlements across Island Melanesia and Micronesia (Panel A) and rank-size distribution across 91 habitation centres showing upper-half power-law scaling ($\alpha = 0,35$, $R^2 = 0,92$, Panel B), 10000BC to 1850.</figcaption>
</figure>

The Mariana Islands (11.999,6 km² mask; roughly 1.007 km² dry land) experienced the most dramatic boom-and-bust trajectory in the entire region. Settled earliest in Remote Oceania around 1500BC at Unai Bapot on Saipan (1.475 by 1650), Taga on Tinian (2.150 by 1668) and Mochong on Rota (1.325 by 1668) [@clark2009radiocarbon; @carson2014first; @pugach2020ancient], Chamorro society expanded from 6k in 1500BC to 24k in 1AD (7,1% share), 33,7k in 1000AD and a pre-contact *latte*-era peak of 42k in 1650—exceeding 41 inhabitants per km² of dry land across Guam, Tinian, Saipan and Rota [@rainbird2004archaeology]. Following the arrival of Jesuit missionaries and Spanish troops in 1668, armed resistance, forced relocation (*reducción*) of northern islanders into consolidated southern Guam parishes (Hagåtña, Agat, Umatac, Merizo, Inarajan and later Sumay) and repeated smallpox and influenza epidemics collapsed the archipelago's population to barely 3.600 Chamorros in 1710, recovering only partially through Filipino and Mexican intermarriage to 9,5k by 1850 (1,6% share; 0,79 inhabitants per km² of mask, the lowest density in the chapter).

Immediately southwest, the Western Carolines of Palau and Yap (5.880,2 km² mask; roughly 560 km² dry land) recorded the highest areal mask density in the entire study at 1850 (6,46 inhabitants per km², equivalent to nearly 68 inhabitants per km² of dry land). Populated by 1000BC (8k), Palau and Yap climbed to 26k in 1AD (7,7% share), 31,9k in 1000AD, 36,5k in 1650 and 38k in 1850 (6,3% share), supported by 9 catalogued settlements [@rainbird2004archaeology; @liu2022ancient]. On Babeldaob in Palau, monumental hilltop earthworks at Ngerdubech (1.415) and stone-monolith ceremonial grounds at Badrulchau (1.485) preceded coastal village confederations led by Koror (2.650 in 1783) and Melekeok (1.890) [@fitzpatrick2010critique; @nunn2010defending]. On Yap, stratified chiefly estates at Gagil-Tomil (4.120 in 1800, the largest single recorded settlement district in our gazetteer) and Rull (2.940) presided over the *sawei* tribute network extending eastward to Falalop on Ulithi Atoll (890) and dispatched ocean-going canoes to Palau to quarry aragonite stone money (*rai*).

The Central-Eastern Carolines encompassing Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae (7.075,7 km² mask; roughly 575 km² dry land) ranked second in 1850 mask density at 5,94 inhabitants per km² (73 per km² of dry land). Uninhabited prior to late first-millennium BC Nuclear Micronesian settlement, the region reached 16k in 1AD (4,7% share), doubled to 32k by 1000AD (6,6%), climbed to 39,4k in 1650 and reached 42k in 1850 (6,9% share) across 8 catalogued centres [@rainbird2004archaeology; @liu2022ancient]. High-island breadfruit, yam and swamp-taro surplus powered Micronesian monumentalism: Pohnpei's Saudeleur capital at Nan Madol housed roughly 1.180 elites and retainers by 1600 before political decentralisation elevated districts such as Kitti (3.120 in 1835), while Kosrae's Leluh fortress held 1.650 inhabitants in 1824 prior to mid-nineteenth-century whaler-borne epidemics. In Chuuk Lagoon, Weno (2.850), Fefan (1.740) and Tonoas (1.680) formed dense volcanic-island clusters, complemented to the south by Polynesian outlier atolls at Kapingamarangi (386) and Nukuoro (212).

Finally, the eastern coral-atoll worlds of the Marshall Islands (17.307,3 km² mask; 181 km² dry land) and the Gilbert Islands with Nauru (9.695,9 km² mask; 307 km² dry land) demonstrate the true carrying capacity of equatorial reef ecosystems once mid-Holocene sea levels fell [@rainbird2004archaeology; @sear2026how]. The Marshalls doubled from 6,5k in 1AD (1,9% share) to 12k in 1000AD and reached 15k by 1850 (2,5% share; 0,87 per km² of buffered mask, yet 83 inhabitants per km² of actual emergent coral land), anchored across 5 catalogued atolls led by Ine on Arno (1.580), Laura on Majuro (1.460), Woja on Ailinglaplap (1.380), Ebon (1.160) and Taroa on Maloelap (960). Even denser, the Gilbert Islands with raised-phosphate Nauru and Banaba rose from 12k in 1AD (3,6% share) to 24k in 1000AD and 31k in 1850 (5,1% share; 3,2 per km² of mask, exceeding 100 inhabitants per km² of dry coral land). Through intensive *babai* (*Cyrtosperma*) pit cultivation, toddy tapping and egalitarian *maneaba* governance, southern and central Gilbertese atolls supported large compact settlements at Utiroa on Tabiteuea (3.850 in 1841), Teaoraereke on Tarawa (2.850), Butaritari (2.420), Tabukiniberu on Beru (2.180) and Kariatebike on Abemama (2.150), alongside Buada on Nauru (1.420) and Banaba (510).

Two structural patterns stand out across Table \ref{tab:regional-shares} and Figure \ref{fig:melanesia-hierarchy}. First, site recovery density per 10.000 km² of mask peaks sharply in compact, intensively surveyed archipelagos—Temotu (24,42), Western Carolines (15,31), Central-Eastern Carolines (11,31) and the Marianas (9,17)—and dips in larger Melanesian landmasses such as the Main Solomons (1,85) and New Caledonia (2,58), confirming why regional headcounts cannot be derived by raw site summation. Second, the 91-site rank-size distribution exhibits a distinctly flat, polycentric upper tail ($\alpha = 0,35$, $R^2 = 0,92$ across the top 45 centres; full 91-site slope $\alpha = 0,73$, $R^2 = 0,66$). Unlike continental empires crowned by a single primate metropolis, oceanic geography capped individual pre-colonial settlements between 2.000 and 4.120 inhabitants—determined by lagoon transport radius, freshwater lens limits and taro-garden catchment—producing a broad plateau of roughly twenty competing island capitals and regional chiefdom seats rather than a steep urban pyramid [@cochrane2021using; @rainbird2004archaeology].

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties govern pre-colonial demographic reconstruction in Island Melanesia and Micronesia.

First, early European contact arrived asymmetrically across the ten sub-regions, creating uneven pre-census depopulation baselines. Whereas Spanish conquest and epidemic mortality struck the Mariana Islands in the late seventeenth century—fully documented in colonial rolls prior to 1850—introduced diseases hit Kosrae, Pohnpei, Aneityum, Tanna, Fiji and New Caledonia primarily during the early and mid-nineteenth century via sandalwooders, whalers and labour recruiters. Back-projecting 1850 totals from 1880s colonial censuses therefore carries an uncertainty band of roughly $\pm 15\%$ to $\pm 25\%$ across interior Melanesia and the outer Carolines.

Second, sub-pixel island geometry limits gridded raster validation in Micronesia. Standard 5-arcminute global land masks fail to resolve small volcanic islets and coral atolls, returning 0 raster inhabitants across all five Micronesian sub-regions despite well-attested pre-colonial populations totalling 161,3k in 1650 and 135,5k in 1850. Conversely, circular maritime buffers needed to display tiny islands on regional maps inflate nominal mask area relative to emergent dry land, requiring careful distinction between mask densities (0,79 to 6,46 inhabitants per km²) and true terrestrial densities (3,46 to over 100 inhabitants per km²).

Third, radiocarbon reservoir offsets and Holocene coastal dynamics affect early colonisation chronologies [@petchey2001radiocarbon; @petchey2019importance; @carson2014first]. Marine shell and lagoonal bone dates require localised $\Delta R$ corrections, while mid-Holocene sea-level drawdown (+1,5 to +2 m above modern mean sea level) and tectonic uplift or subsidence across the Vanuatu and Solomon arcs have buried or eroded early Lapita beach middens [@sear2026how; @bedford2011lapita]. Similarly, the summary cache's backward clamping of post-Lapita initial values across earlier benchmark columns produces nominal pre-1AD totals (109k at 10000BC, 143k at 1500BC) that must always be read alongside the raw zero-floor archaeological onset schedule.

Fourth, pre-colonial settlement figures aggregate culturally diverse residential units. Compact fortified islands such as Bau (3.500) and stone-walled complexes such as Leluh (1.650) or Nan Madol (1.180) represent physically bounded nucleated towns, whereas high-ranking entries such as Gagil-Tomil (4.120), Kitti (3.120) or Anelgauhat (3.513) represent closely integrated village-district clusters sharing a single chiefly ceremonial precinct and irrigated valley catchment.

# Conclusion

Between 10000BC and 1850, Island Melanesia and Micronesia experienced one of the most remarkable maritime expansions in human history. Beginning with barely 8k Pleistocene inhabitants in the Main Solomon Islands while nine-tenths of the basin lay empty, two independent Austronesian seafaring breakthroughs—the 1500BC crossing to the Mariana Islands and the 1100BC to 850BC Lapita expansion across Remote Oceania—joined by subsequent Near Oceanic gene flow and Nuclear Micronesian atoll settlement filled every habitable archipelago by 1AD with 338k inhabitants [@clark2009radiocarbon; @sheppard2011lapita; @lipson2018population; @liu2022ancient].

Over the next sixteen centuries, landscape engineering—irrigated taro terraces in New Caledonia and Vanuatu, ring-ditch deltas in Fiji, *latte* villages in the Marianas, basalt-megalithic compounds at Nan Madol and Leluh, and *Cyrtosperma* pit horticulture across equatorial atolls—lifted the regional total to 487,3k in 1000AD and 601,5k in 1650 [@rainbird2004archaeology; @anonymous2009early]. By 1850, the eve of comprehensive European colonial partition, the region stood at 606,5k inhabitants: 471k (77,7%) across Fiji (145k), the Main Solomons (135k), Vanuatu (115k), New Caledonia (65k) and Temotu (11k), and 135,5k (22,3%) across the Central-Eastern Carolines (42k), Western Carolines (38k), Gilberts and Nauru (31k), Marshalls (15k) and the severely depopulated Marianas (9,5k). Across 91 catalogued centres capped around 2.000 to 4.120 inhabitants, this polycentric maritime demography set the baseline from which nineteenth-century epidemic shocks and twentieth-century Pacific urbanisation would later unfold.

# Footnotes

Note 1. Geographic naming follows contemporary regional usage paired with historical colonial equivalents where relevant: Vanuatu corresponds to the former New Hebrides, Kiribati encompasses the Gilbert Islands and Banaba, and the Main Solomon Islands sub-region includes the autonomous island province of Bougainville and Buka Island within Papua New Guinea because they form a single Pleistocene biogeographic chain (Greater Bukida).

Note 2. Pre-1AD headline totals in the automated summary cache (109k at 10000BC, 143k at 1500BC and 156,2k at 1000BC) reflect backward clamping of each sub-region's initial non-zero benchmark onto earlier time slices for continuous trajectory plotting. Active human population grounded in calibrated radiocarbon onset stood at 8k in 10000BC, 48k in 1500BC and 121,7k in 1000BC, converging identically with the cache at 338k from 1AD onward.

Note 3. Buffered archipelago mask area (220.891,8 km²) includes coastal maritime halos around small volcanic islands and coral atolls to ensure legible cartographic rendering. Dry-land densities quoted in prose divide regional populations by emergent terrestrial area derived from archival cadastral and hydrographic baselines.
